questions.q: According to the NCERT textbook, which of the following is NOT presented as a common factor uniting all nations worldwide: common descent, common language, common religion, or common political ideals?
questions.a: Correct answer: Common political ideals is NOT listed as a universal common factor; the textbook explicitly states "Neither descent, nor language, nor religion or ethnicity can claim to be a common factor in nationalisms all over the world" and identifies shared political ideals as a CHOICE democracies make, not a given. A wrong answer (e.g., picking "common descent") reveals the student still holds the primordialist misconception that nations are naturally given by birth/ethnicity, missing the constructivist argument that nations are "imagined communities" (Anderson, node 005) held together by collective belief.

questions.q: The NCERT text states: "Nationalist struggles have contributed to the drawing and redrawing of the boundaries of states and empires." Explain why the principle of national self-determination, when applied after WWI (Treaty of Versailles) and after decolonization, led to BOTH the creation of new states AND new minority problems.
questions.a: Correct answer: The "one culture-one state" principle proved impossible to implement cleanly because populations were intermingled; drawing boundaries to match cultural lines inevitably left minorities on the "wrong" side, creating irredentism and displacement (e.g., partition of India, population exchanges in Europe). A wrong answer that only mentions "new states were created" misses the analytical core: self-determination contains an internal contradiction—granting it to Group A often denies it to Group B within the same territory. This reveals failure to grasp the "paradox of self-determination" central to node 006 and 007.

questions.q: A student argues: "Indian nationalism was essentially Hindu nationalism because the movement used Hindu symbols (Bharat Mata, Vande Mataram) and the Muslim League demanded Pakistan." Using the NCERT framework of civic vs ethnic nationalism (node 003) and the text's discussion of "shared political ideals," construct a counter-argument citing TWO specific Congress resolutions or actions that demonstrate the civic nationalist strand.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) 1929 Lahore Congress Purna Swaraj resolution declaring independence for "India" as a whole, not a Hindu nation; (2) 1931 Karachi Resolution on Fundamental Rights guaranteeing religious freedom, equality before law, and minority protections—explicitly framing nationhood in political-legal terms. A weak answer that only says "Gandhi was secular" fails to cite institutional evidence. This tests whether the student can distinguish between cultural symbols used for mobilization (which exist in all nationalisms) and the constitutional-political architecture of the imagined community—key to node 003 and 009.

questions.q: Compare the Basque case study (NCERT p.105) with the Indian anti-colonial struggle. Identify ONE structural similarity and ONE fundamental difference in their claims to self-determination, using the concepts of "territory," "historical identity," and "political ideals."
questions.a: Correct answer: Similarity—both claim a distinct historical identity and territory (Basque fueros/autonomy; India's civilizational continuity) as basis for self-rule. Difference—Basque nationalism is primarily ethnic-cultural (language, race, distinct institutions); Indian nationalism explicitly adopted civic-political ideals (democracy, secularism, composite culture) as the binding principle, rejecting "one culture-one state." A wrong answer conflating both as "ethnic" misses the textbook's central argument that anti-colonial nationalism in Asia/Africa redefined self-determination as democratic inclusion, not cultural purity. This reveals inability to apply the civic/ethnic distinction (node 003) to concrete cases.

questions.q: Evaluate Tagore's critique (NCERT p.108-109): "I will never allow patriotism to triumph over humanity." Is this a rejection of anti-colonial nationalism per se, or a warning against a specific deformation of it? Justify with reference to his distinction between "opposing western imperialism" and "rejecting western civilisation."
questions.a: Correct answer: Tagore supported anti-colonial nationalism (opposed British rule, renounced knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh) but warned against xenophobic, inward-looking nationalism that defines itself by hatred of the "other"—what he saw in the Swadeshi movement's boycott of all things Western including science, education, and universal humanism. His distinction shows he feared nationalism becoming a "cult of the nation" (ethnic/cultural purity) rather than a vehicle for human dignity. A wrong answer calling Tagore "anti-national" or "pro-British" reveals a binary misunderstanding: that critique of nationalism's excesses equals opposition to freedom. This is a senior-secondary error—confusing normative political theory with partisan loyalty.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word preamble for a hypothetical "Declaration of Indian National Identity" (c. 1930) that embodies the CIVIC nationalist vision described in NCERT—incorporating territory, shared political ideals, historical identity, and pluralism—WITHOUT invoking any single religion, language, or ethnicity as the basis of unity.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) name the territory (Indian subcontinent), (2) invoke civilizational continuity without religious ownership ("ancient land of diverse philosophies"), (3) pledge allegiance to democratic self-government, secular citizenship, equal rights, (4) explicitly recognize linguistic/cultural/religious diversity as constitutive, not incidental, (5) ground legitimacy in popular sovereignty. A weak answer that includes "Hindu-Muslim unity" as the basis, or "Sanskrit as national language," or "Vedic heritage" as the sole source, fails the civic nationalism test—it reproduces the ethnic/cultural definition the textbook argues against. This reveals whether the student can operationalize the theoretical distinction in a constitutive document.
